changes.after: The same moment can have different calendar dates in different time zones.

before:
The JVM java.time.Instant represents a point on the time line. ZoneId supplies rules for presenting that instant as local calendar time. Converting with atZone preserves the instant, not necessarily its displayed date.

Instant.parse takes ISO instant text such as "2025-01-01T00:30:00Z" and returns an Instant; Z identifies UTC. ZoneId.of takes a zone-ID String such as "UTC" or "America/New_York" and returns the corresponding ZoneId rules object. These are the inputs to the existing atZone calls.

At 00:30 UTC on January 1, New York is still on December 31. toLocalDate extracts the date from each zoned representation. This example uses JVM java.time rather than claiming a multiplatform date API or reading the current clock.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneId

fun main() {
    val instant = Instant.parse("2025-01-01T00:30:00Z")
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("UTC")).toLocalDate())
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")).toLocalDate())
}
```

Expected output or behavior: 2025-01-01
2024-12-31. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why a date without time or zone is insufficient to identify a global instant. You may trace it without a Kotlin compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An Instant represents one moment on the timeline. `Instant.parse` reads that moment from text. The Z at the end means UTC, the shared time reference used here.
A time zone gives the rules for a place's local clock. `ZoneId.of` finds those rules by name. The call atZone shows the same moment in that zone. The call toLocalDate takes just its calendar date.

Follow the example one line at a time.
```kotlin
import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneId

fun main() {
    val instant = Instant.parse("2025-01-01T00:30:00Z")
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("UTC")).toLocalDate())
    println(instant.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")).toLocalDate())
}
```
The screen shows `2025-01-01`, then `2024-12-31`. At 00:30 UTC on January 1, New York is five hours behind and still on December 31.
Changing the zone changes how the moment is shown, not the moment itself. A date alone cannot identify one exact moment worldwide. This JVM example uses a fixed input, not the current clock.
